892: The three-way interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 81.12% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 65.71% by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months, a spread of 15.41 percentage points. This range appreciably exceeded that generated by any single factor in isolation, the three factors having operated jointly; a favourable outcome therefore required all three to be specified concurrently.
901: Starch constitutes the principal component of the rice grain and the primary source of its food energy. Birbhum and Howrah returned the highest starch content at 72.97%, followed by Nadia at 72.69% and Purba Bardhaman at 72.35%, Nadia proving on par with both of the others; the entire spread amounted to only 0.62 percentage points. Since starch forms the bulk of the grain, its proportion varies comparatively little from field to field, and a narrow location effect is therefore the expected outcome. Zhou et al. (2015) placed this process at the centre of their account of rice ageing, while Zia-Ur-Rehman (2006) similarly determined that the extent of starch loss in stored cereals is contingent upon both the grain itself and the conditions of the store, reporting almost no loss where grain was held at 10 °C.
905: Location exerted a highly significant effect on amylose. The highest value, 19.32%, was recorded at Purba Bardhaman, followed by Nadia with 18.77% and Birbhum/Howrah with 18.73%. Nadia and Birbhum/Howrah shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, while a margin of 0.58 percentage points separated the superior location from the inferior.
907: The landraces likewise differed significantly, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 19.38%, followed by Radhunipagal with 18.87% and Gobindabhog with 18.58%. No two landraces shared a letter group, Kalojira exceeding Gobindabhog by 0.80 percentage points.
909: Storage period altered amylose significantly at the 1% level. In order of sampling, the values were 17.77% in fresh paddy, 18.48% at 4 months, 19.46% at 8 months and 20.05% at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 12 months and the minimum in fresh paddy. Over the full year the value increased by 12.8%.
911: The location × variety interaction was non-significant. Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 19.74%, and Gobindabhog at Nadia the inferior one with 18.36%. The varietal order Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog remained invariant across locations; the interaction therefore altered the magnitude of the varietal margin but not its sign.
912: Location and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean, 20.38%, was recorded for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months and the lowest, 17.42%, for Birbhum/Howrah in fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +12.3% at Nadia, +11.6% at Purba Bardhaman and +14.6% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations shifted by nearly equivalent margins, the district of production exerting negligible influence on the action of storage.
913: The variety × storage interaction was non-significant. The highest mean, 20.39%, was recorded for Kalojira at 12 months and the lowest, 17.38%, for Gobindabhog in fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +13.5% in Gobindabhog, +13.5% in Radhunipagal and +11.5% in Kalojira. All three changed by comparable margins and thus responded to storage in a uniform manner.
914: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 20.68% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months, and the minimum of 17.10% by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled as fresh paddy. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
923: Amylose governs the mouthfeel of cooked rice: rice low in amylose cooks moist and sticky, whereas rice of higher amylose content cooks drier and firmer (Mutters and Thompson, 2009). Purba Bardhaman returned the highest amylose at 19.31% and differed significantly from Nadia at 18.77% and from Birbhum and Howrah at 18.73%, the latter two being on par with each other. In the freshly harvested condition all three landraces fell within the low-amylose class of 12 to 20% delimited by Juliano (1992). The location effect, although significant, was small, and Li et al. (2018) likewise concluded that amylose is determined more by genotype than by environment. Okpala et al. (2020) found that low temperature during grain filling elevated both amylose percentage and the elongation of cooked rice, which suggests that the locational differences in amylose observed here derive in part from differences in ripening temperature among the districts.
927: Location exerted a highly significant effect on soluble protein. The highest value, 1.319%, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Birbhum/Howrah with 1.232% and Purba Bardhaman with 1.154%. The three locations resolved into discrete groups, each differing significantly from the others, the spread from the superior to the inferior site amounting to 0.165 percentage points.
929: The three landraces likewise differed, the varietal effect being highly significant. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value, 1.267%, followed by Radhunipagal with 1.219% and Kalojira with 1.218%. Radhunipagal and Kalojira shared a common letter and were thus on par with each other, while Gobindabhog exceeded Kalojira by 0.049 percentage points.
931: Storage period altered soluble protein significantly at the 1% level. In order of sampling, the values were 1.518% in fresh paddy, 1.368% at 4 months, 1.163% at 8 months and 0.890% at 12 months, fresh paddy standing highest and the 12-month sample lowest. The value declined by 41.4% over the year.
933: Location and variety did not operate independently, their interaction being highly significant. Gobindabhog at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 1.396%, and Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 1.084%. The landraces did not retain the same order at every location: at Nadia the order ran Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira; at Purba Bardhaman, Radhunipagal, Kalojira, Gobindabhog; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Radhunipagal. Rank reversal of this kind indicates a differential response to the growing environment.
934: The location × storage interaction was non-significant. The highest mean, 1.584%, was recorded for Nadia in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.802%, for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. From fresh paddy to 12 months the value shifted by -39.0% at Nadia, -44.9% at Purba Bardhaman and -40.5% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change scarcely differed between locations, storage having elicited an equivalent response in grain of all three provenances.
935: No significant interaction emerged between variety and storage. The highest mean, 1.557%, was recorded for Gobindabhog in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.863%, for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -40.2%, Radhunipagal by -42.9% and Kalojira by -41.0%. The magnitude of change was comparable in all three landraces, storage having acted upon them equivalently.
936: The three-factor interaction attained the 1% level. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 1.707% was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 0.781% by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months, a spread of 0.926 percentage points. No single factor in isolation generated a range of this width; location, landrace and storage acted in combination, and the optimum outcome was attainable only through the appropriate conjunction of all three.
945: Soluble protein represents that fraction of the grain protein extractable into solution. The location effect is plausibly attributable to differences in soil nitrogen and in temperature during grain filling. Li et al. (2018) determined that environment outweighed genotype in respect of protein content and reported that warmer weather during ripening elevated grain protein. The underlying mechanism is well established: Chrastil and Zarins (1992) demonstrated that storage induces the formation of sulphur bridges within the principal rice protein and drives the smaller fractions into larger aggregates. Such aggregates dissolve less readily, so that the assay registers less protein even though the nitrogen content of the grain has scarcely altered. This distinction is material to the interpretation of the result, since the nutritional value may indeed decline even where total protein remains unchanged.
949: Location exerted a highly significant effect on fat. The highest value, 1.207%, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 1.149% and Birbhum/Howrah with 1.144%. Purba Bardhaman and Birbhum/Howrah shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, with 0.063 percentage points separating the extremes.
951: The three landraces also differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 1.256%, followed by Gobindabhog with 1.215% and Radhunipagal with 1.028%. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 0.228 percentage points.
953: Storage period altered fat to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 1.382% in fresh paddy, 1.239% at 4 months, 1.095% at 8 months and 0.950% at 12 months, the maximum falling on fresh paddy and the minimum on 12 months. A decline of 31.3% was registered over the full year.
955: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Kalojira at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 1.313%, and Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 0.953%. An identical varietal sequence (Kalojira first, Gobindabhog second and Radhunipagal third) obtained at all three sites; the interaction therefore modified the magnitude of the varietal differences while leaving their direction intact.
956: No significant interaction arose between location and storage. The highest mean, 1.421%, was recorded for Nadia in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.931%, for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months. Over 12 months of storage the change amounted to -31.2% at Nadia, -30.8% at Purba Bardhaman and -31.8% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change was comparable across locations, storage having been conducted at a single site and having acted uniformly on grain of every provenance.
957: The variety × storage interaction was significant at the 1% level. The highest mean, 1.491%, was recorded for Kalojira in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.832%, for Radhunipagal at 12 months. The twelve-month change amounted to -31.5% in Gobindabhog, -31.0% in Radhunipagal and -31.2% in Kalojira. None of the three shifted appreciably more than the others, and no differential response to storage was detected among them.
958: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 1.558% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 0.743% by Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
967: Rice contains only a small proportion of fat, yet that fraction exerts an influence on flavour and storage life disproportionate to its quantity. The greater part of rice lipid is located in the bran and the embryo, so the location effect observed here reflects differences in the thickness of these layers and in the residue remaining after polishing. Genkawa et al. (2008) noted that fat acidity rises rapidly in stored rice and is widely employed on that account as an index of the extent of grain deterioration. Kim et al. (2023) corroborated this in a recent study of post-harvest handling, in which fat acidity and sensory quality both deteriorated progressively as storage temperature and storage period increased. The low-molecular-weight compounds generated on oxidation of rice lipid impart the stale odour characteristic of old rice and act antagonistically to whatever aroma persists in the grain; Zhou et al. (2002) described the same association between lipid breakdown and flavour change in stored rice.
971: Location exerted a highly significant effect on ash. The highest value, 0.828%, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Birbhum/Howrah with 0.824% and Purba Bardhaman with 0.697%. Each location occupied a discrete letter group, matching neither of the others, and the superior and inferior locations differed by 0.131 percentage points.
973: The three landraces likewise differed, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 0.989%, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.767% and Gobindabhog with 0.593%. The three landraces resolved into discrete groups, Kalojira exceeding Gobindabhog by 0.396 percentage points.
